activities.anchor: A chart is not an illustration of an argument
activities.caption: file each device under honest or misleading
activities.name: chartsHonestSort

config.prompt: File each device under the chart it belongs to:

items.label: aligning the encoding with the data's importance
grey for everything except the story
dual axes slid into an apparent relationship

config.why: Dishonest charts mislead without a single false word — which is why chart literacy is an ethics skill as much as a design one.

activities.anchor: The scientific foundation is Cleveland and McGill's experiments
activities.caption: pair each encoding with how well eyes judge it
activities.name: chartsPercepMatch

config.prompt: Pair each encoding with its judging accuracy:

pairs.right: judged most accurately — your most important variable belongs here
nearly as well — the bar's channel
judged poorly — the pie chart's problem
worst of all — rough, secondary distinctions only

config.why: The hierarchy, not a preference: scatter beats bubble, grouped bar beats pie, and 'which slice is bigger?' is a question pies answer badly.

activities.anchor: Chart type follows question type, mechanically
activities.caption: fill the blanks — the question-to-chart map
activities.name: chartsTypeCloze

config.text: Chart type follows question type: comparison across categories → a %%0%% chart, sorted by value; trend over time → a %%1%% chart; the relationship between two quantities → a %%2%% plot; part-to-whole → stacked bars or a 100% bar.
config.hint: Length for comparing, position over time for trending, two axes for relating.

activities.caption: call the lie factor of the famous chart
activities.name: chartsLieEst

config.prompt: Tufte's fuel-economy chart drew its effect nearly how many times larger than the real mpg increase?
config.why: A lie factor of 9.4 — the measure matters because it removes intent from the question: a misleading chart is misleading whether or not anyone meant it.
config.context: 1.0 would be a chart that shows exactly what the data says

activities.anchor: spurious-correlation factory; the honest use demands
activities.caption: bet before you read on — testing the twin slopes
activities.name: chartsDualPredict

config.q: Two lines rise together on a dual-axis chart. What single check tests whether the connection is real?
choices: Rescale one axis — if the 'correlation' changes with your zoom, the chart was the correlation
Compute the correlation coefficient of the two series
Extend the window by five more years
config.why: With dual axes you can slide one scale until any two series move in apparent lockstep — a claim that survives only at one zoom was never a claim about the data.

activities.anchor: The palette failure modes are known
activities.caption: find the backwards habit — spending colour
activities.name: chartsColourSpot

config.prompt: One of these colour habits is backwards — click it:
lines: One accent colour for the thing you are talking about, grey for everything else.
Rainbow scales create fake boundaries in smooth data.
Red-green defaults fail roughly one reader in twelve.
Encode meaning in hue alone to keep the chart clean.
config.correction: Never encode meaning in hue alone — use colourblind-safe sequential palettes (viridis and relatives) and back colour with position or labels.
config.why: Colour is one of the encodings: readers assume the most urgent colour marks the most important data, so spend colour on the story or not at all.

activities.anchor: A chart without explanation makes the reader write the explanation
activities.caption: caption versus conclusion — drag the divider
activities.name: chartsTitleCompare

config.prompt: Two titles for the same chart — drag the divider:

before.label: 'Sales by region'
before.text: a caption — the reader arrives unpointed and writes their own story from their priors

after.label: 'Region C drives the decline'
after.text: a conclusion — the reader arrives pointed at what the chart actually shows

config.why: The title is a conclusion, not a caption — and if you cannot state a finding, the chart may not have one, which is worth knowing before you present it.

activities.anchor: The redesign: horizontal bars from zero
activities.caption: rebuild the redesign, step by step
activities.name: chartsRedesignOrder

config.prompt: Rebuild the honest redesign in order:
items: One accent colour on the largest, grey on the rest
Direct value labels and a title stating the finding
config.why: The honest chart read 'Growth is flat across regions' — the opposite of the original's visual story: truncation did not just exaggerate, it manufactured drama that did not exist.

activities.anchor: The five-question audit takes a minute
activities.caption: audit the news graphic
activities.name: chartsAuditBranch

config.root: A news graphic shows a dramatic doubling since 2019. You have one minute.

choices.label: Where does the axis start?
choices.feedback: Truncation renders rounding errors as cliffs — would the story survive a zero baseline?

choices.label: Where does the window start and end?
choices.feedback: Start points are choices — a line from the all-time peak tells a different story than the same line from the trough.

choices.label: What is the denominator?
choices.feedback: Percent of what — the base of a percentage is where most chart tricks actually live.

axis.text: From zero the doubling may be a 4% rise — the cliff was the axis, not the world.

window.text: Ask why those dates: defensible on the data's own terms, or on the argument's?

denominator.text: 'Doubling' of a share, of a rate, of a count? Each is a different claim — and only one may be true.

config.why: The encoding is the claim, and the claim deserves to be read — ten minutes of re-plotting is the fact-checking of the visual age.
